[0] everyday_reading (E): Everyday writing is drafted all at once and revised at the end. A program is grown in small steps from a version that already works, compiling and running after each step.
[1] misconception (M) -> WriteAllThenTest: wrong rule: Write the whole program first, then compile and test it all at the end. Right rule: Start with a working program and make small changes, compiling and testing after each one, so an error is always in the last change.
[2] inconsistent_trace (T) -> WriteAllThenTest: Applies incremental development unevenly: tests the first few steps one at a time, then adds a large block of untested code at once. (here mixing in: "Write the whole program first, then compile and test it all at the end")

[0] names_the_element (N): Incremental development: growing a program in small, tested steps from a version that works.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Start with a working program and make small, incremental changes; at any point, if there is an error, you will know where to look. Use variables for intermediate values so you can check them.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Sequencing: write a few lines, compile, run and check them, then add the next few; never more than one untested change at a time.
[1] output_prediction (OP): Result: after every step there is a program that compiles and runs, and does a little more than before.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): State transition: one step adds a small piece of code and ends with the program compiling and passing its checks again.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): Running after each step shows at once whether the new lines do what was intended.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): Small steps make debugging local: the newest change is the first suspect.
[2] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Plan: keep a working program at all times so that errors are found where they are made.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> WriteAllThenTest: Conservation: each step must keep everything that already worked; if a step breaks it, that step is undone or fixed before going on.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): For any new program: get a minimal version running first (even just printing the inputs), then add one feature at a time, testing each.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Compile and test after each small change. Kind: compile-time or logic error. Trigger class: many lines are written before the first compile, so the messages and wrong outputs cannot be traced to one change

wrong: Write the whole program first, then compile and test it all at the end. | right: Start with a working program and make small changes, compiling and testing after each one, so an error is always in the last change.
Developing in small steps keeps debugging local: an error is in the change just made.
Each small step is run and checked before the next one is added.
